title: Remotes & Push
subtitle: Connect your repo to GitHub and share your work
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Your commits exist only on your machine. If your laptop dies, the work is gone. Your teammates can't see your code. You can't deploy.
whyItExists.solution: A remote is a copy of your repo hosted elsewhere (GitHub, GitLab, etc.). git push uploads your commits to the remote so they're backed up and shared.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Push frequently — at least daily. Push before stepping away. Push before submitting a PR.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't push broken code to main. Don't force-push shared branches without team agreement.

explainModes.beginner: A remote is your repo on GitHub. git push sends your commits up to GitHub. Think of it as saving to the cloud. git remote add origin <url> is how you connect a new local repo to GitHub.
explainModes.simple: git remote add origin <url> — links your repo to GitHub. git push origin main — sends commits to GitHub. git push -u origin main — same, but also sets 'origin/main' as the default so future pushes are just git push. git remote -v — shows your remotes.
explainModes.standard: A remote is just a URL with a name (usually 'origin'). You can have multiple remotes. git push <remote> <branch> uploads local branch commits to the remote. The -u flag sets upstream tracking — subsequent git push/pull know where to go without specifying. git push --force-with-lease is safer than --force (won't overwrite if someone else pushed).
explainModes.technical: Remote tracking branches (origin/main) are local references that mirror the remote's state at the last fetch/pull. git push updates the remote and advances the remote tracking branch. HTTPS authentication now uses personal access tokens (PATs) or credential helpers. SSH uses ed25519 key pairs — faster and no token expiry. git remote set-url origin <new-url> changes an existing remote's URL.
explainModes.deepDive: Git's push protocol negotiates which objects the remote needs (missing commits, trees, blobs), then sends a packfile. The receive-pack hook on the server validates and integrates the push. Protected branches on GitHub use server-side hooks to enforce rules (required reviews, status checks). git push --tags pushes annotated tags (lightweight tags aren't pushed by default). Git LFS (Large File Storage) is a git push extension for pushing large binary files.

content.code:
# See existing remotes
git remote -v
# origin  https://github.com/prashantkeshr/KERNAL.git (fetch)
# origin  https://github.com/prashantkeshr/KERNAL.git (push)

# Add a remote (for a fresh git init repo)
git remote add origin https://github.com/yourname/my-project.git

# Change a remote URL (e.g., after repo rename)
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/yourname/new-name.git

# Remove a remote
git remote remove origin

# Add a second remote (e.g., for deploying to a different host)
git remote add deploy https://git.heroku.com/my-app.git

# First push — set upstream tracking with -u
git push -u origin main
# From now on, just:
git push

# Push a specific branch
git push origin feature/login

# Push all branches
git push origin --all

# Push tags
git push origin --tags

# Delete a remote branch
git push origin --delete feature/old-branch

# Safe force push (fails if remote has new commits you haven't seen)
git push --force-with-lease

# 1. Create repo on GitHub (via github.com UI)

# 2. Init local project
mkdir my-project && cd my-project
git init
git switch -c main   # or: git config init.defaultBranch main

# 3. Add files and commit
echo '# My Project' > README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Initial commit"

# 4. Connect to GitHub
git remote add origin https://github.com/yourname/my-project.git

# 5. Push
git push -u origin main

questions.question: What does git push -u origin main do differently from git push?
options: It sets origin/main as the upstream so future git push/pull commands work without arguments
questions.explanation: The -u (or --set-upstream) flag tracks the remote branch. After git push -u origin main, you can just type git push (no remote or branch name needed) and Git knows where to push.

faq.q: Why is my push rejected with 'Updates were rejected'?
faq.a: The remote has commits you don't have locally. Someone else pushed first, or you pushed from another machine. Run git pull (or git fetch + git merge) to bring those commits in, then push again.

faq.q: HTTPS vs SSH — which should I use?
faq.a: HTTPS is easier to set up. Use a personal access token (PAT) as the password. SSH requires generating an ed25519 key pair and adding the public key to GitHub settings — but once done, it's seamless: no password prompts, no token rotation.
